_comment: Language-neutral conformance corpus for the QTerm runtime (issue #159).
Three published packages implement the same builder API and must agree:
quiltlang (crates.io), quilt-python (PyPI) and quilt-wasm (npm). Each has a
thin runner that walks these cases against its native API, so a divergence
is a test failure rather than something a user discovers.
A term is a tagged object:
{"leaf": {"tag": t, "text": s}}   {"sym": s}   {"name": s}
{"qlift": v}                        {"qlift_html": v}
{"quote"|"unquote": {tag, index, lang, term, cmds}}
A step is {"w": s} | {"c": term} | {"e": term} | {"p": s} | "n" | "x".
A cmd is  {"write": s} | {"push": s} | "NL" | "POP" | "HOLE".
`runtimes` narrows a case to the implementations that have the API; omit it
to mean all three. Every narrowing needs a `why`, so a gap is a recorded
decision and not an accident.
`checks` are the cross-cutting ones: instead of a term and its expected
text, a check is a property every case's term must satisfy, so it covers
each shape in the corpus without restating any of them. Each names the
runtimes that have the API it needs, with the same `why` obligation. A
runner must fail on a check that names it and that it does not implement —
adding one here is a request the runners cannot silently ignore.
The governing law for lift is ↓(↑(x)) == x: ↑ maps a value to a term whose
code evaluates back to it. These cases compare coparse() text, which cannot
see that law directly — checking it needs the reduce backends, so it lives
in the nightly job. A case that records behaviour known to *violate* the law
it is right.
The lift law is reduce(lift(x)) == x: lift maps a value to a term whose code
evaluates back to it, so lifting a *term* yields constructor code. All three
runtimes satisfy it as of #166; the eval-based checks that prove it live in
the Python and Node runners, which can actually evaluate the generated code.

checks.name: postcard_roundtrip
checks.why: quilt-wasm exposes no postcard entry points; quilt-python has the pair (postcard_bytes / from_postcard_bytes), and the Rust side owns the serde derives both ends decode with
checks.what: from_postcard_bytes(postcard_bytes(x)) coparses to the same text as x, and re-serializes to the same bytes. This pair is the wire format of the heterogeneous reduce protocol and neither half had a test. Covered: every shape the corpus builds survives the round trip, and the two derives stay inverses of each other - postcard is positional and self-describes nothing, so an asymmetry decodes as a *different term* rather than as an error. Not covered: a *symmetric* schema change. The corpus constructs its terms, so their QTerm::span is always None, and a serde(skip) on both ends round-trips cleanly here while breaking the cross-process protocol the field's no-skip comment warns about. Only a parsed term carries a span and only Rust can build one, so that case is a Rust test - qterm::tests::postcard_round_trip_preserves_spans.

checks.name: stringify_agrees_with_coparse
checks.why: Rust has no Display impl on QTerm, so it has nothing that could disagree with coparse. Python spells this str(x) (__str__) and quilt-wasm spells it toString
checks.what: The runtime's native stringification is coparse. Both are exported and a caller may reasonably reach for either - in JS every string interpolation reaches for toString implicitly - so the two must not drift apart.

cases.name: qlift_float_integral_keeps_its_point
cases.why: 1.0 formatted with to_string() is '1' in Rust, which would lift a float as an integer literal and silently change the generated code's type

cases.name: qlift_float_integral_drops_its_point_in_ts
cases.why: Deliberately different, and correct for the target: every JS number is a double, so `1` and `1.0` are the same value and `fmt_number` drops the point so whole numbers read as integer literals. The distinction only matters in a language with separate int and float types

cases.name: qlift_bool
cases.why: Rust and TypeScript both spell the literal `true`; Python spells it `True`, so that case is separate rather than pretending the three agree

cases.name: qlift_bool_python_spelling
cases.why: Python's boolean literal is `True`. This case exists because the runtime used to return `1`: bool is an int subclass, so extract::<i64> matched first and silently generated an integer where the author wrote a boolean

cases.name: qlift_string_with_quote
cases.why: the escaping bug #144 found in QLift for str: a bare `"` produced a literal that does not reparse

cases.name: qlift_on_term_builds_constructor_code
cases.why: Lifting a term must yield code that *reconstructs* it, so that reduce(lift(x)) == x. All three runtimes agree on the leaf shorthand. See issue #166.

cases.name: qlift_on_term_builder_chain_rust
cases.why: Same law; the builder chain differs only in Rust's `.c(&child)` — its builder takes `&Arc<QTerm>` where the Python and wasm runtimes take the term by value. That divergence is documented and deliberate.

cases.name: qlift_on_term_builder_chain_by_value
cases.why: Same law; the builder chain differs only in Rust's `.c(&child)` — its builder takes `&Arc<QTerm>` where the Python and wasm runtimes take the term by value. That divergence is documented and deliberate.

cases.name: qlift_html_int
cases.why: no LiftTo<Html> marker exists on the Rust side — issue #149

cases.name: qlift_html_escapes_markup
cases.why: no LiftTo<Html> marker exists on the Rust side — issue #149

cases.name: qlift_html_escapes_both_attribute_quotings
cases.why: no LiftTo<Html> marker exists on the Rust side — issue #149. The apostrophe was the one entry in the escape table with no coverage in either binding (issue #192): a hole inside `title='…'` breaks out of the attribute exactly the way `"` does inside a double-quoted one

cases.name: qlift_html_is_idempotent_on_terms
cases.why: no LiftTo<Html> marker exists on the Rust side — issue #149

cases.name: unicode_content_survives
cases.why: the runtime must not apply Quilt's own glyph escaping to target text
